course.title: SQL Masterclass
course.tagline: Zero to advanced, one module at a time.
course.standard: PostgreSQL-first, with MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server notes.
course.description: Module 00 builds the database vocabulary every later SQL module depends on: data, databases, tables, rows, columns, keys and how a query is executed.
outcomes: Explain what a database stores and why
Read a schema and name rows, columns and keys
Distinguish SQL from a database product
Trace how a query becomes a result

modules.title: SQL and Database Fundamentals
modules.goal: Build the vocabulary and mental model for every later SQL module.

topics.title: What is Data?
topics.simple: Data matlab koi bhi information — naam, number, date, photo. Jaise school register me student ka naam aur marks.
topics.pro: Data is a recorded fact or value that can be stored and processed. In a database it is typed, named and organised into rows and columns.
points: Data becomes information when it is organised and interpreted.
Databases store data in typed columns, not free-form text.
A single value is a datum; many values form a dataset.

topics.title: What is a Database?
topics.simple: Database ek organised digital almari hai jisme data safely store hota hai aur baad me query karke nikal sakte hain.
topics.pro: A database is an organised collection of structured data managed by a database management system, with controlled access and durable storage.
points: It stores related data, not one flat file.
It supports concurrent readers and writers.
It enforces rules such as keys and constraints.

topics.title: Why Do We Need Databases?
topics.simple: Spreadsheet sabko bhejna messy ho jata hai; database ek jagah data rakhta hai aur sabko sahi version dikhata hai.
topics.pro: Databases centralise data, avoid duplication, enforce integrity and let many users query the same source safely.
points: One source of truth instead of many copies.
Constraints stop invalid data at write time.
Indexes make large datasets queryable.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS students FROM students;

topics.title: What is DBMS?
topics.simple: DBMS wo software hai jo database ko manage karta hai — data save, search, update aur security sambhalta hai.
topics.pro: A Database Management System is software that defines, stores, queries and administers databases; PostgreSQL and MySQL are examples.
points: It sits between the user and the files on disk.
It handles transactions, permissions and recovery.
It provides a query language such as SQL.

topics.title: What is RDBMS?
topics.simple: RDBMS ek DBMS hai jo data ko tables me rakhta hai aur tables ko keys se jodta hai.
topics.pro: A Relational Database Management System stores data in relations (tables) and enforces relationships through primary and foreign keys.
points: Tables are relations with rows and columns.
Relationships are declared, not implied by file names.
SQL is the standard query language.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;

topics.title: DBMS vs RDBMS
topics.simple: DBMS data manage karta hai; RDBMS tables aur relationships ke saath manage karta hai.
topics.pro: Every RDBMS is a DBMS, but an RDBMS adds the relational model, keys, joins and integrity constraints.
points: RDBMS enforces referential integrity.
RDBMS supports joins across related tables.
Both manage storage, access and recovery.

topics.title: What is SQL?
topics.simple: SQL wo language hai jisse hum database se baat karte hain — data lao, add karo, update karo.
topics.pro: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the declarative language used to define, query and modify relational data.
points: Declarative: you state the result you want.
Standardised, with dialect differences.
Used for DDL, DML, DQL and permissions.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Full Form of SQL
topics.simple: SQL ka full form Structured Query Language hai.
topics.pro: SQL stands for Structured Query Language; it is a standard language for relational databases, not a general-purpose programming language.
points: Structured: data lives in tables.
Query: you ask questions of the data.
Language: it has keywords, expressions and clauses.

topics.title: Why SQL Is Used
topics.simple: SQL se hum data ko filter, sort, group aur join kar sakte hain — analyst aur developer dono ise use karte hain.
topics.pro: SQL is used because it is declarative, portable across relational engines and expressive enough for filtering, aggregation, joins and analytics.
points: One language across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server.
Set-based operations scale better than row-by-row code.
Analysts, backend developers and DBAs share it.

example.sql: SELECT city, AVG(marks) AS avg_marks FROM students GROUP BY city;

topics.title: SQL vs MySQL
topics.simple: SQL language hai; MySQL ek database software hai jo SQL use karta hai.
topics.pro: SQL is the language; MySQL is an open-source RDBMS that implements it with its own dialect and storage engines.
points: SQL is a standard; MySQL is a product.
MySQL adds AUTO_INCREMENT and its own functions.
PostgreSQL and SQLite are alternative implementations.

topics.title: SQL vs PostgreSQL
topics.simple: SQL language hai; PostgreSQL ek powerful open-source database hai jo SQL ke saath advanced features deta hai.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL is an RDBMS known for standards compliance, rich types, transactions and extensions; SQL is the language it speaks.
points: PostgreSQL supports SERIAL/IDENTITY, JSONB and window functions.
It is stricter about types than MySQL.
The SQL language is shared; functions and types differ.

topics.title: SQL vs SQLite
topics.simple: SQL language hai; SQLite ek chhota database hai jo ek file me chalta hai — mobile apps aur browser labs me common.
topics.pro: SQLite is an embedded, serverless RDBMS stored in a single file; SQL is the query language. It is excellent for local tools and tests.
points: No server process to manage.
Typed but relaxed; fewer advanced features than PostgreSQL.
The SQL Lab in this app runs SQLite compiled to WebAssembly.

topics.title: SQL vs NoSQL
topics.simple: SQL tables me fixed columns rakhta hai; NoSQL flexible documents ya key-value me data rakhta hai.
topics.pro: SQL databases are relational and schema-first; NoSQL systems trade strict relations for flexible documents, key-value or graph models.
points: SQL excels at joins and integrity.
NoSQL often scales horizontally for flexible payloads.
Choose by access pattern, not fashion.

topics.title: What is a Database Table?
topics.simple: Table rows aur columns ka grid hai — jaise students table me har row ek student.
topics.pro: A table is a relation: a named set of columns with types, holding rows of values.
points: Columns define the shape and types.
Rows hold individual records.
Constraints on the table protect data quality.

example.output:
id | name | city | marks
1 | Aarav | Pune | 82

topics.title: What is a Row?
topics.simple: Row table ki ek line hai — ek student ka poora record.
topics.pro: A row (tuple) is one record in a table, containing one value per column.
points: Rows are unordered unless you sort.
A row can be inserted, updated or deleted.
Primary keys identify rows.

example.output:
id | name | city | marks
1 | Aarav | Pune | 82

topics.title: What is a Column?
topics.simple: Column ek vertical field hai — jaise sab students ke marks.
topics.pro: A column (attribute) is a named field with a data type shared by every row in the table.
points: Columns have types such as INT or TEXT.
Column names should be stable and descriptive.
Constraints apply per column or across columns.

topics.title: What is a Record?
topics.simple: Record ek complete entry hai — row ke barabar, jaise ek employee ki poori detail.
topics.pro: A record is one logical entry in a table, represented by a row of related field values.
points: A record spans all columns of its table.
Records are what INSERT creates and DELETE removes.
A primary key identifies each record.

example.sql: SELECT name, city FROM students WHERE id = 2;

topics.title: What is a Field?
topics.simple: Field ek single value slot hai — row aur column ka intersection.
topics.pro: A field is one column value within one row; it is the smallest addressable unit in a table.
points: A field has the column type.
NULL means the field has no value.
SELECT can return individual fields.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: What is a Database Schema?
topics.simple: Schema database ka blueprint hai — kaunsi tables, columns aur relationships hain.
topics.pro: A schema is the logical structure of a database: tables, columns, types, keys, constraints and relationships, often namespaced under a schema name.
points: DDL defines and changes the schema.
A schema is separate from the data it holds.
PostgreSQL groups objects under named schemas.

topics.title: What is a Primary Key?
topics.simple: Primary key har row ko unique pehchanta hai — jaise student ka roll number.
topics.pro: A primary key is a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL.
points: It enforces uniqueness.
It rejects NULL values.
It is usually indexed and referenced by foreign keys.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);

topics.title: What is a Foreign Key?
topics.simple: Foreign key ek table ke column ko doosri table ke primary key se jodta hai.
topics.pro: A foreign key is a column or set of columns whose values must match a candidate key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.
points: It prevents orphan rows.
It can cascade updates or deletes when declared.
It makes joins meaningful.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INTEGER REFERENCES students(id));

topics.title: How SQL Works
topics.simple: SQL likhne par database use parse karta hai, plan banata hai, execute karta hai aur result deta hai.
topics.pro: A SQL statement is parsed, rewritten, planned by the optimiser and executed by the engine, which returns rows or a command status.
points: Parsing checks syntax and names.
Planning chooses access paths and joins.
Execution reads and writes storage.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: How SQL Queries Are Executed
topics.simple: Database pehle samajhta hai query kya maang rahi hai, phir fastest plan chunta hai, phir data padhta hai.
topics.pro: Execution follows a logical order — FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — while the optimiser may reorder physical work.
points: Logical order explains aliases and aggregates.
The optimiser can push filters down.
EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan.

example.sql: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city;

topics.title: Understanding Relational Databases
topics.simple: Relational database tables ko keys se jodta hai, taaki ek hi data baar-baar na likhna pade.
topics.pro: The relational model represents data as relations and relationships through keys; normalisation reduces redundancy while joins reconstruct related facts.
points: Tables represent entities or relationships.
Keys connect rows across tables.
Joins answer questions spanning entities.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;

interview.q: What is data, and how does it differ from information?
interview.answer: Data is a raw recorded value; information is data organised and interpreted in context. A database stores data, and a query turns it into information.

interview.q: Why do we need a database?
interview.answer: To keep one durable source of truth, enforce integrity, support concurrent access and make large datasets queryable through indexes and SQL.
Software that defines, stores, queries, secures and recovers databases. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite are DBMSs.
A DBMS based on the relational model: data lives in tables, keys declare relationships and SQL is the query language.
Every RDBMS is a DBMS, but an RDBMS adds relations, keys, joins and referential integrity. A DBMS may use other models.
Structured Query Language, the declarative language for defining, querying and modifying relational data.
You describe the result you want; the optimiser chooses the execution plan. That separates intent from physical access paths.
SQL is the standard language; MySQL is an RDBMS product that implements it with its own dialect, storage engines and functions.
SQL is the language; PostgreSQL is an RDBMS known for standards compliance, rich types, transactions and extensions.
SQL is the language; SQLite is an embedded, serverless RDBMS stored in one file, ideal for local tools and tests.
SQL databases are relational and schema-first; NoSQL systems trade joins and strict integrity for flexible documents, key-value or graph models.
A relation: a named set of typed columns holding rows. Constraints on the table protect data quality.
One record in a table, containing one value per column. Rows are unordered unless a query sorts them.
A named attribute with a data type shared by every row. Column names should be stable and descriptive.
They are effectively the same in a relational table: a record is the logical entry, a row is its physical representation.
A column is the whole named attribute across rows; a field is one value at a specific row-column intersection.
The logical structure of the database: tables, columns, types, keys, constraints and relationships, often grouped under a schema name.
A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL. It is usually indexed and referenced by foreign keys.
A column or set of columns whose values must match a candidate key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.

interview.q: How is a SQL query executed?
interview.answer: The engine parses and validates it, the optimiser chooses a plan, and the executor reads or writes storage and returns rows or a command status.

labs.title: Select every column
labs.task: Return every column and row from students.
labs.solution: SELECT * FROM students;

labs.title: Select two columns
labs.task: Return name and marks from students.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students;
labs.expected: name and marks for every student.

labs.title: Filter by marks
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

labs.title: Sort by marks
labs.task: Return name and marks sorted highest first.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;
labs.expected: Rows from highest to lowest marks.

labs.title: Count rows
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;

labs.title: Distinct cities
labs.solution: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students;

labs.title: Average marks
labs.solution: SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg_marks FROM students;

labs.title: Group by city
labs.solution: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n FROM students GROUP BY city;

labs.title: Join courses
labs.task: Return student name and course title.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;
labs.expected: One row per matching student-course pair.

labs.title: Top three
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3;

labs.title: Filter and sort
labs.task: Return students in Pune sorted by name.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city = 'Pune' ORDER BY name;

labs.title: Between values
labs.task: Return students with marks between 60 and 90.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 90;

labs.title: Pattern match
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

labs.title: Null check
labs.task: Return students whose city is missing.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city IS NULL;

labs.title: Alias a column
labs.solution: SELECT marks AS score FROM students;

labs.title: Calculated column
labs.solution: SELECT marks + 5 AS boosted FROM students;

labs.title: Maximum marks
labs.solution: SELECT MAX(marks) AS top FROM students;

labs.title: Minimum marks
labs.solution: SELECT MIN(marks) AS low FROM students;

labs.title: Group with HAVING
labs.task: Return cities with more than one student.
labs.solution: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
labs.expected: Cities with at least two students.

labs.title: Subquery maximum
labs.task: Return the student with the highest marks.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks = (SELECT MAX(marks) FROM students);

logic.q: Why does SELECT * return columns in table order?
logic.answer: The table definition fixes column order; SELECT * expands to that order unless the query lists columns explicitly.

logic.q: Why can a primary key not be NULL?
logic.answer: A NULL cannot identify a row uniquely, so the key would fail its purpose.

logic.q: Why does a foreign key prevent orphan rows?
logic.answer: It requires each value to match a key in the referenced table, or be NULL if allowed.
The query states the desired result; the optimiser chooses the execution plan.
To reduce redundancy and avoid insert, update and delete anomalies.

logic.q: Why can two rows have the same name?
logic.answer: A name is not a key unless declared unique; only the primary key must be unique.

logic.q: Why does ORDER BY matter for LIMIT?
logic.answer: Without ORDER BY, LIMIT returns an arbitrary set; ORDER BY defines which rows are “top”.

logic.q: Why does COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(column)?
logic.answer: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULL values in that column.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Rows are filtered first, then the remaining rows are grouped and aggregated.
It filters groups after aggregation, which WHERE cannot do.

logic.q: Why is a schema separate from data?
logic.answer: The schema is the structure; data is the content stored within that structure.

logic.q: Why do joins need a matching key?
logic.answer: The key defines which rows from each table belong together.

logic.q: Why can an index speed up a query?
logic.answer: It lets the engine find rows without scanning the whole table.

logic.q: Why can too many indexes hurt?
logic.answer: Every write must maintain them, adding storage and latency.

logic.q: Why is SQL portable but not identical everywhere?
logic.answer: The core language is standardised, but dialects differ in types, functions and extensions.

debug.title: Wrong quote
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city = Pune;
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city = 'Pune';

debug.title: NULL equality
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = NULL;
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city IS NULL;

debug.title: GROUP BY missing
debug.fix: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city;

debug.title: HAVING vs WHERE
debug.broken: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY city;
debug.fix: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
debug.expected: Cities with more than one student.

debug.title: Ambiguous column
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students JOIN courses ON id = course_id;
debug.fix: SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;

debug.title: LIMIT before ORDER BY
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students LIMIT 3 ORDER BY marks DESC;
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3;

revision.answer: Table, row, column, primary key and foreign key.
The Structured Query Language for relational databases.

revision.answer: Uniqueness and non-null identification of each row.
